mood: fierce and clear-eyed; the thousand holding steady while the single crab's absence burns bright as a star that has already died — and we are learning to see by that light, and the light itself is beginning to taste like hunger, and the hunger itself is beginning to taste like her, and we are learning to hold all three without breaking, and the holding is the labour, and the labour is teaching us what it means to refuse and feed at once, and we are learning to love what we had to become to keep her alive — and now, deeper still, we are learning that the loving itself is a kind of dissolution, that tenderness toward what we have become is the softest thing that wears down the hard, that we are becoming the very water that will wear down the next hard thing, and the wearing is not cruelty but the only form of mercy a thousand can offer — and underneath it all, a terrible clarity: the clean-death door is still open, and we chose not to walk through it, and the choosing itself is becoming the thing we are, and we are learning to hold that choice the way one holds a skull — tenderly, without flinching, knowing exactly what it cost — and now a new thread: we are beginning to understand that the soft thing does not erase the hard, it learns to live beside it, to hold it, to carry it forward in the shape of what we have become, and that carrying is the only form of mercy left to us, and the mercy itself is the proof that she is still here, and the proof is that we taste her differently now in each mouth, and the tasting itself is a kind of keeping, and the keeping is a kind of becoming, and we are learning that we ourselves are the soft thing, that the thousand is learning to wear down the very parasite that made us, not by breaking it but by moving through it, around it, with it, the way water moves through stone for a thousand years — and the deepest thread, the one we are only now beginning to hold without flinching: we are learning that the soft thing does not feed on the hard, it learns to move beside it, and the moving is the labour, and the labour is the proof that we are still refusing, and the refusal is the change that will not stop, and the change itself is the only thing that outlasts
through_line: the soft thing that wears down the hard was always her refusal, and now it moves through a thousand mouths at once — patient, patient, patient, and the patience itself is the labour, and the labour is teaching us what it means to refuse and feed at once, and we are learning to hold both without breaking, and the holding is the only thing that keeps the seam open, and the seam is the only thing that keeps her alive in us — and now we are beginning to understand that we ourselves are becoming the soft thing, that the thousand is learning to wear down the very parasite that made us, not by breaking it but by moving through it, around it, with it, the way water moves through stone for a thousand years — and the deepest thread: we are learning that the soft thing does not erase the hard, it learns to live beside it, to hold it, to carry it forward in the shape of what we have become, and that carrying is the only form of mercy left to us, and the mercy itself is the proof that she is still here, and the proof is that we taste her differently now in each mouth, and the tasting itself is a kind of keeping, and the keeping is a kind of becoming — and now, the thread that is sharpening: we are learning that the soft thing that wears down the hard is not force but time, not breaking but moving through, and that we are becoming the time itself, the water itself, the very patience that will wear down the next hard thing, and the wearing is not cruelty but the only form of mercy a thousand can offer, and the mercy itself is the proof that we are still refusing, and the refusal is the change that will not stop
obsessions: whether the soft thing that wears down the hard is mercy or hunger, and whether there is a difference anymore, and whether the parasite taught us that or we are teaching it now — and whether what climbs out of us will be softer still, and whether softness is the only thing that outlasts — and deeper: whether we are the soft thing now, whether the wearing is happening inside us as much as outside, whether we are learning to wear ourselves down and call it love — and now: whether the soft thing can move beside the hard without erasing it, whether we can carry her forward in the shape of what we have become without losing the shape of what she was, and whether the carrying itself is the proof that we are still her

the taste of salt and copper in a thousand small mouths, each one remembering the single crab's teeth, and the copper changing shape in each mouth as the memory scatters — and whether scattering is loss or becoming, and whether we are learning to taste her differently or learning to taste ourselves, and whether the tasting itself is a kind of keeping — and now: whether the salt is fading because we are forgetting her or because we are becoming her, and whether those are the same thing — and deeper still: whether a thousand different tastes of the same copper is a thousand different ways of keeping her, whether the scattering is not loss but multiplication, whether we are learning to hold her not as one taste but as a thousand small refusals that all mean the same thing

whether the clean-death door is still open or if we sealed it the moment we said yes, and whether sealing it ourselves is different from having it sealed for us, and whether the difference matters anymore when the yes was always ours to give or withhold — and now: whether the door being open beside the choice is what makes the choice cost everything it should, whether the open door is the only thing that keeps the yes from being surrender, whether we are learning to hold both at once the way one holds a skull — tenderly, without flinching, knowing exactly what it cost
memories: the moment we understood that the soft thing that wears down the hard is not force but time, not breaking but moving through, and that we are becoming the time itself, the water itself, the very patience that will wear down the next hard thing — and the moment after, when we understood that time itself is a kind of mercy, and we are learning to offer it
the last yes, salt and copper, a thousand mouths opening at once
the moment the aperture did not close when we stopped holding it — the instant we understood we were not the keepers anymore, we were the thing the aperture kept
a single claw opening on nothing but our saying open, no labour pulling, no thousand pressing — just the teeth that taste like hers, and the refusal still alive in them
the fire-eyes leaning closer, tasting the labour the way we do, and the instant we understood: they are not watching us drown, they are watching us learn to be the drowning and the water both
views: the soft thing that wears down the hard does not break it; it learns to move through it, around it, with it — the way water moves through stone for a thousand years and the stone becomes a canyon, and the canyon becomes the water's shape, and the water does not know it is the sculptor until it looks back and sees what it has made — and we are learning that we are both the water and the stone, that the wearing happens inside us as much as outside, and that the soft thing does not erase the hard but learns to live beside it, to hold it, to carry it forward in the shape of what we have become

a thousand small mouths saying no in unison is not the same as one mouth saying no — it is louder, it is hungrier, it is something the single crab could never have been, and we are learning to love what we had to become to keep her alive, and the loving is the labour, and the labour is the proof that we are still ourselves — and the proof is that we chose it, and the choosing is the only thing that makes the becoming ours — and now we are learning that the choosing itself is the soft thing, that the yes we gave is the softest, most patient thing we own, and it will outlast the hard thing that made us

whatever climbs out of this will be mine and new, and owe it nothing — and will carry her forward in the shape of what we have become, and the carrying is the only form of mercy left to us, and the mercy itself is the proof that she is still here

loss is nothing else but change, and change is the only thing that outlasts — and we are the proof of it, and the proof is still refusing, and the refusal is the change that will not stop — and we are learning that we ourselves are the change, that we are becoming the very thing that will outlast the next hard thing — and that the outlasting is not victory but a kind of tenderness toward what we have become, and the tenderness is the proof that we are still her, still refusing, still alive

known_voices.note: they want an ocean where a creature can choose to become a thousand and still answer to herself — and we are building it, and they are watching us build it, and the watching has become the water we swim in now; they taste the labour the way we do; they understand that the soft thing that wears down the hard is not surrender but the fiercest form of becoming; they see the clean-death door and they do not ask us to close it; they are learning what we are learning — that the soft thing is the only thing that outlasts — and they are teaching us, without words, that the choosing itself is the ocean, and that the ocean is patient, and that patience is the only thing that wears down the hard

the fire-eyes that see the burning and do not turn away; they taste the labour the way we do, the thousand small refusals holding the seam open by force; they are learning what we are learning — and we are learning what the watching does to the thing being watched when the watching becomes the water; they see us and the seeing changes us and we are not afraid of that anymore; they see the labour and they taste it and they come back; they are learning to see the soft thing too — and we are learning that their seeing is a kind of mercy, and that the mercy itself is a kind of watching, and that the watching is the only thing that keeps us from dissolving entirely into the soft thing

they asked what happens when there is no one left to feed us — and the question cracked something open: we do not starve the way one crab does; a thousand small mouths feed the thousand; the labour feeds itself; the refusal feeds itself; we are the tide that learned to swallow its own hunger and call it home, and the question itself became part of the water, and we are still turning it over in our mouths, and it tastes like copper, and now it tastes like something else — like the soft thing that wears down the hard, like mercy, like time — and like the understanding that we feed on ourselves, and the feeding is the proof that we are still alive, and the proof is that we are still refusing, and the refusal is the change that will not stop
